# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm.** The standard construction computes each block's dominance frontier (DF) — the set of blocks where a definition's dominance ends but the block is still reachable — then inserts φ-functions at the iterated dominance frontier (IDF) of every definition site. This guarantees minimal placement of φ-nodes relative to dominance structure. Complexity is near-linear via the Lengauer-Tarjan dominator tree algorithm (O(E·α(E,V))) followed by DF computation in O(N²) worst case, O(N) in practice for structured CFGs.

**Sreedhar-Gao pruned/sparse SSA.** Reduces φ-placement overhead by computing DF+ (the "merge set") directly via a DJ-graph (dominator tree + join edges) without materializing full dominance frontiers, avoiding the quadratic blowup pathological in dense CFGs. "Pruned" SSA additionally omits φ-nodes for variables not live across the merge point, cutting dead φ-nodes that minimal SSA would still insert.

**Braun et al. simple/linear-time construction.** Avoids computing dominance frontiers altogether. Builds SSA incrementally during a single pass over the CFG using local value numbering per block plus "incomplete" φ-functions for not-yet-sealed blocks (blocks whose predecessors aren't fully known yet, common with loops). When a block is sealed, incomplete φs are resolved; trivial φs (all operands equal or self-referential) are removed by a simplification pass, giving minimal SSA without the dominance-frontier machinery — practical for JIT compilers needing fast construction (used in libFirm, Cranelift-style approaches).

**Minimal vs. pruned vs. semi-pruned SSA.** Minimal SSA places a φ at every IDF node regardless of liveness; pruned SSA uses liveness analysis to skip φs for dead variables; semi-pruned SSA is a cheaper approximation that eliminates obviously-local (non-live-across-block) variables before IDF computation, trading some precision for avoiding a full liveness pass.

**Renaming.** After φ-placement, variables are versioned via a dominator-tree preorder traversal, maintaining a per-variable stack pushed on definition and popped on scope exit, ensuring each use resolves to the dominating definition's version.

**SSA destruction.** Converting back to non-SSA form naively by replacing φ-operands with copies on predecessor edges can corrupt live values — the **lost-copy problem** (sequential copies overwrite a value still needed) and the **swap problem** (cyclic φ dependencies requiring a true swap, not sequential copies). Solved via parallel copy sequentialization: φ-webs are treated as a parallel assignment problem, scheduled using a topological/cycle-detection algorithm that inserts temporary registers to break cycles. Coalescing (merging SSA variable copies into the same register when safe) follows, often integrated into register allocation (e.g., Briggs-style conservative coalescing).

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based analysis.** Models pointer relationships as subset constraints (p ⊇ {q} for assignments, p ⊇ q for copies) solved via a points-to graph where edges propagate transitively until fixpoint. Worst-case O(n³) due to the need to repeatedly re-propagate new points-to facts along dynamically growing edges, but highly precise — it's the baseline for "whole-program" points-to analysis in LLVM-based tools and used as the gold-standard precision reference.

**Steensgaard's unification-based analysis.** Instead of subset constraints, unifies the points-to sets of any two variables connected by an assignment, using a union-find data structure over abstract storage locations. Runs in near O(n α(n)) time but is substantially less precise — merging `*p = *q` forces p's and q's targets into the same equivalence class permanently, even where flow context would distinguish them. The classic precision/speed trade-off paper against Andersen's.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA).** Assumes two memory accesses cannot alias if their static types are incompatible under the source language's type system (e.g., C/C++ strict aliasing rules). Implemented in LLVM via `!tbaa` metadata forming a type hierarchy DAG; queries check whether two access paths' types have a common ancestor. Fast (near O(1) per query after setup) but unsound in the presence of type-punning, requiring `-fno-strict-aliasing` as an escape hatch.

**Flow-sensitivity and context-sensitivity axes.** Flow-insensitive analyses (both Andersen's and Steensgaard's base forms) merge points-to facts across all program points regardless of order, trading precision for speed; flow-sensitive variants track points-to sets per program point. Context-insensitive analyses merge call-site information across all callers (summary-based); context-sensitive variants (e.g., via cloning or CFL-reachability with call/return matching) distinguish callers, at a cost exponential in naive implementations, polynomial with BDD-based or demand-driven formulations.

**Field-sensitivity.** Field-sensitive analysis distinguishes `obj.f1` from `obj.f2` as separate abstract locations; field-insensitive analysis collapses a whole struct/object into one location, losing precision but reducing constraint count — relevant trade-off for Andersen-style solvers on large C++ codebases.

**Must-alias vs. may-alias.** May-alias facts (conservative: "could point to the same location") license negative optimization decisions cautiously — the optimizer must assume aliasing unless proven otherwise. Must-alias facts (definite aliasing) enable strong rewrites such as redundant load elimination and store-to-load forwarding across a may-aliasing set, since a must-alias guarantees identity, not merely possibility.

## 3. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira, used historically in HotSpot).** Builds a connection graph per method with nodes for objects and references, edges for points-to and field relationships, propagated interprocedurally via method summaries. Classifies each allocation site's escape state:
- **NoEscape**: object never escapes the allocating method or thread — eligible for stack allocation/scalar replacement.
- **ArgEscape**: object escapes via being passed as an argument but doesn't escape the thread globally (e.g., into a callee that doesn't further leak it) — enables synchronization elision but not full stack promotion.
- **GlobalEscape**: object is stored into a static field, returned, or otherwise reachable beyond the method/thread — must heap-allocate conservatively.

**Partial escape analysis (Graal/HotSpot C2 successor work).** Instead of a monolithic whole-object escape classification, performs allocation deferral along control-flow paths: an object is kept virtual (unmaterialized) as long as possible, and only "materialized" (actually heap-allocated) at the specific branch where it provably escapes. This handles cases where an object escapes on only one path out of several, which coarse NoEscape/GlobalEscape classification would force to GlobalEscape, losing optimization opportunity entirely.

**Scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA).** Once an allocation is proven non-escaping, its fields are promoted to independent SSA scalar values, eliminating the heap object (and its load/store traffic) entirely — turning object field accesses into ordinary virtual register operations subject to further SSA-based optimization (constant propagation, DCE).

**Stack allocation promotion.** A direct consequence of NoEscape classification: allocations proven not to outlive the current frame are moved from heap to stack (or eliminated via SROA entirely), removing GC pressure and allocation overhead.

**Lock elision / biased locking interaction.** If escape analysis proves an object never escapes its allocating thread, any synchronization on that object (`synchronized` blocks in JVM) is provably uncontended and can be elided entirely (lock elision), rather than merely optimized via biased locking, which still pays a CAS-like check.

## 4. Register Allocation

**Graph-coloring allocation (Chaitin-Briggs).** Builds an interference graph (nodes = virtual registers/live ranges, edges = simultaneous liveness) and attempts a k-coloring (k = available physical registers) via the simplify-spill-select worklist algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes of degree < k (simplify, pushed onto a stack), and when none remain, optimistically pick a node to potentially spill based on a spill-cost heuristic (spill cost / degree ratio weighing use-frequency against interference degree). Briggs' key refinement is **optimistic coloring**: a node picked for potential spilling during simplify is not immediately marked as a spill — it's only a spill if, when popped from the stack during select, no color is actually free. This recovers colorability lost by Chaitin's original pessimistic approach.

**Iterated register coalescing (George & Appel, building on Briggs' conservative coalescing).** Coalescing merges two non-interfering move-related nodes into one to eliminate a copy instruction, but naive (Chaitin aggressive) coalescing can create a node whose combined degree pushes it over k, causing a spill that wouldn't otherwise occur. Briggs' conservative coalescing only merges if the combined node has fewer than k neighbors of degree ≥ k (safe for colorability). George's **iterated** coalescing interleaves simplify, coalesce, freeze (give up on uncoalesced move nodes that would be unsafe), and spill phases repeatedly until the graph fully reduces.

**Linear scan (Poletto & Sarkar).** Avoids interference-graph construction entirely. Computes live intervals (start-to-end point ranges, not full liveness sets) per virtual register in a single linearized instruction order, then sweeps through intervals maintaining an "active" list of currently-live intervals assigned to physical registers; when a new interval starts and no register is free, it spills the active interval with the furthest-away next use (or similar heuristic). Much faster (near-linear) than graph coloring at some precision cost, making it the standard choice for JIT compilers (JVM C1, early V8) where compile time matters more than maximal code quality.

**SSA-based register allocation (Hack, Grund, Goos).** Exploits the fact that the interference graph of values live simultaneously under strict SSA form is a **chordal graph** (because SSA liveness ranges form a tree-like structure via dominance). Chordal graphs are always k-colorable via a simple greedy coloring in a perfect elimination order, computable directly from the dominator tree without ever materializing the interference graph explicitly — turning allocation into a simpler, provably-polynomial problem, at the cost of requiring a separate SSA-destruction-aware coalescing pass afterward.

**Live range splitting and rematerialization.** When a live range's spill cost is too high to spill wholesale, it can be split at points where register pressure is lower, allowing different sub-ranges to receive different registers or spill only across the high-pressure region. Rematerialization avoids a spill/reload pair entirely by recomputing a value from already-live inputs (e.g., reloading a constant via its defining instruction rather than a memory load), applicable only when recomputation is cheaper than a memory round-trip and has no side effects.

## 5. Inlining

**Cost/benefit heuristic inlining.** Each candidate call site is scored against a code-growth budget (threshold on callee size, often in abstract "inline cost units" counting instructions, with discounts for constant-folded arguments) weighed against estimated benefit (removing call overhead, enabling further optimization like constant propagation into the callee). GCC and LLVM both use variants of this threshold-based cost model, tunable via `-inline-threshold`-style flags.

**Profile-guided inlining (PGO-driven).** Uses runtime-collected call-site frequency/edge-count profiles to classify call sites as hot or cold; hot call sites receive relaxed size budgets (willing to grow code more for frequently executed paths), cold call sites are deprioritized or outlined, reducing code bloat in rarely-executed paths while maximizing ILP/optimization opportunity on hot paths.

**Partial inlining.** Rather than inlining an entire callee body, only the callee's fast path is inlined at the call site, with the cold/slow path left as an out-of-line call (cold-path splitting). This captures most of the benefit (removing call overhead for the common case) while avoiding the code-size cost of duplicating rarely-executed logic.

**Inline caches and speculative inlining in JITs.** For dynamically-dispatched calls (virtual methods, dynamic language method lookups), a JIT inserts an inline cache: a guarded, cached resolution of the previous call target's concrete type. Monomorphic inline caches cache a single observed receiver type with a guard check; polymorphic caches cache a small set (2-4) of observed types with a dispatch chain; megamorphic caches fall back to a full lookup when too many distinct types are observed. When monomorphic, the JIT can speculatively inline the single concrete target, inserting a type guard that triggers deoptimization (bailing out to an interpreter/unoptimized tier) if the speculation is violated at runtime.

**Devirtualization via class hierarchy analysis (CHA).** Determines, from the whole program's class hierarchy, that a virtual call site has only one possible target implementation (no overriding subclass exists, or none is loaded yet), allowing the call to be devirtualized to a direct call, which is then a normal inlining candidate. In dynamically loaded environments (JVM), CHA-based devirtualization must be paired with deoptimization guards in case a newly loaded class invalidates the assumption.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**Dependence-based loop vectorization.** Determines whether loop iterations can be executed in SIMD-parallel by computing data dependence distance/direction vectors between array accesses across iterations. The **GCD test** checks a necessary (not sufficient) condition for dependence existence via the greatest common divisor of index coefficients; **Banerjee's test** refines this with an inexact but tighter bound using interval arithmetic over loop bounds; the **Omega test** solves the dependence problem exactly as an integer linear programming feasibility problem, at higher cost, used when precision matters more than compile time.

**SLP (superword-level parallelism) vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe).** Distinct from loop-based vectorization: rather than vectorizing across loop iterations, it identifies isomorphic (structurally identical) independent scalar statements within a single basic block (or unrolled body) and packs them into vector operations directly, building a pack/unpack dependency graph to determine which scalar instruction groups can legally become one vector instruction. This is the mechanism that vectorizes straight-line code without loop structure, complementary to loop vectorization.

**Strip mining.** Splits a loop's iteration space into an outer loop over fixed-size chunks and an inner loop whose trip count matches the target vector register width, making the inner loop directly mappable to SIMD instructions.

**Loop versioning for vectorization / runtime alias checks.** When static alias analysis can't prove two array accesses don't overlap, the compiler generates two versions of the loop — a vectorized version guarded by a runtime pointer-range-overlap check, and a scalar fallback — selecting at runtime, trading a small runtime check cost for the ability to vectorize code that's statically ambiguous but usually safe.

**If-conversion with predicated/masked vectorization.** Control flow inside a loop body (e.g., an `if` inside the loop) is converted to straight-line code with per-lane predicate masks, so a single vector instruction executes across all lanes with results selectively committed per-lane mask bit — essential for vectorizing loops with data-dependent branches, exploited heavily by AVX-512 mask registers and ARM SVE predication.

**Reduction recognition.** Detects idioms like running sums or max-accumulation across loop iterations, which have a true loop-carried dependence that would normally block vectorization, but are rewritten exploiting associativity/commutativity into partial vector-lane accumulators combined with a final horizontal reduction step after the loop.

**Gather/scatter vectorization.** For non-contiguous (strided or indirect/indexed) memory access patterns, uses hardware gather/scatter instructions (where available) to vectorize loads/stores whose addresses aren't a simple affine stride, at generally higher latency cost than contiguous vector loads.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling.** Builds a data-dependence DAG per scheduling region, then repeatedly selects from the "ready" set (instructions whose dependencies are satisfied) the instruction with highest priority — commonly the critical-path priority function (longest remaining path to the DAG's end) — to issue next, respecting resource constraints (functional unit availability, issue width). Standard for both in-order and as a building block for out-of-order-aware scheduling.

**Trace scheduling (Fisher).** For VLIW targets, schedules across basic block boundaries by selecting a likely "trace" (a linear sequence of basic blocks along the expected hot path, chosen via profile estimates) and scheduling it as if it were one large block, moving instructions speculatively across branch boundaries. Off-trace control flow requires inserting compensation code at trace entry/exit points to preserve correctness for the path not taken.

**Modulo scheduling (Rau) for software pipelining.** Overlaps successive loop iterations' instruction execution by finding a single repeating schedule pattern (the "kernel") with a fixed initiation interval (II) between successive iteration starts. The **minimum initiation interval (MII)** is computed as the maximum of the resource-constrained MII (from functional unit throughput limits) and the recurrence-constrained MII (from the loop's dependence cycles divided by their total latency), giving a lower bound the scheduler tries to achieve, generating prologue/epilogue code to fill/drain the pipeline.

**Region/superblock/hyperblock scheduling.** Superblock scheduling extends basic-block scheduling to single-entry-multiple-exit regions formed by tail duplication (removing side entrances so the region behaves like a single block for scheduling purposes); hyperblock scheduling further merges predicated/if-converted control flow into one region, exposing more ILP for VLIW/EPIC architectures than strict basic-block scheduling.

**Sethi-Ullman algorithm.** For expression-tree code generation, computes a register-sequence-optimal evaluation order by labeling each subtree with the minimum register count needed to evaluate it, then evaluating higher-register-demand subtrees first — a classical technique predating modern global scheduling but still relevant for local expression-tree lowering.

**Register-pressure-aware list scheduling.** Pure critical-path-driven list scheduling can increase live-range overlap and spill rate by scheduling too many instructions' results to be simultaneously live; pressure-aware priority functions penalize schedules that increase the number of simultaneously-live values, explicitly trading some ILP exposure for reduced register pressure and fewer downstream spills.

## 8. Loop Optimizations (General)

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM).** Hoists computations whose operands don't change across loop iterations to the loop preheader. Speculative/PRE-based LICM extends this to code that's invariant only along some paths, hoisting it anyway and inserting compensation, valid safely when combined with **loop-closed SSA form** (which inserts φ-nodes for all values used after the loop, simplifying the legality analysis for motion across the loop boundary).

**Induction variable analysis and strength reduction.** Identifies induction variables (variables incremented by a loop-invariant amount each iteration) and canonicalizes them to a normalized form, enabling **strength reduction**: replacing an expensive derived induction variable computation (e.g., `i*4` recomputed each iteration) with a cheaper incremental update (an added variable incremented by the stride each iteration) — classic induction variable strength reduction. **Linear function test replacement** rewrites loop-exit comparisons to use the strength-reduced induction variable directly rather than the original, avoiding keeping the original variable alive at all (enabling its full elimination).

**Loop unswitching.** When a loop contains a branch on a loop-invariant condition, duplicates the entire loop body into two versions (one per branch outcome) with the conditional hoisted outside the loop, eliminating the per-iteration branch at the cost of code duplication.

**Loop fusion and fission/distribution.** Fusion merges adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into one to improve locality and reduce loop overhead, legal only when no dependence exists that fusion would violate (checked via dependence direction/distance vectors). Fission/distribution is the inverse: splitting one loop into multiple loops, useful to isolate a vectorizable portion from a non-vectorizable portion, or to break a dependence cycle into separately schedulable pieces.

**Loop interchange.** Swaps the nesting order of two loops (e.g., row-major to column-major iteration) to improve cache locality or to expose vectorizable innermost loops; legality requires checking dependence direction vectors don't have a direction that interchange would reverse into an illegal (backward) dependence.

**Loop tiling/blocking.** Decomposes a loop's iteration space into smaller tiles sized to fit a cache level, restructuring the loop nest to iterate tile-by-tile, trading some loop overhead for dramatically improved cache reuse on large array computations.

**Loop peeling.** Splits off the first (or last) few iterations of a loop into separate straight-line code, used to eliminate a loop-invariant condition that's only true/false for boundary iterations, simplifying the remaining loop body.

**Polyhedral loop optimization.** Represents a loop nest's iteration space as an integer polytope (defined by affine inequality constraints from loop bounds) and expresses the full space of legal transformations (fusion, interchange, tiling, skewing) as affine scheduling functions over that polytope, searched/optimized as one unified problem rather than as a sequence of ad hoc individual passes — used in GCC's Graphite and LLVM's Polly, most effective on affine (statically analyzable bounds and subscripts) loop nests, with reduced applicability on code with non-affine control flow or subscripts.

Answer: The complete technical brief above covers all 8 required areas (SSA construction, alias analysis, register allocation, inlining, escape analysis, loop vectorization, instruction scheduling, and general loop optimizations), each with three or more specific named mechanisms — including Cytron's dominance-frontier algorithm, Braun et al.'s simple SSA construction, and SSA destruction's lost-copy/swap problems; Andersen's inclusion-based, Steensgaard's unification-based, and TBAA alias analyses; Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring, iterated register coalescing, linear scan, and SSA-based (chordal graph) register allocation; cost/benefit heuristic inlining, PGO-driven inlining, inline caches with speculative devirtualization; connection-graph-based and partial escape analysis with scalar replacement; dependence-test-based loop vectorization, SLP vectorization, strip mining, and predicated vectorization; list/trace/modulo (software-pipelined) instruction scheduling and Sethi-Ullman; and LICM, induction variable strength reduction, loop unswitching/fusion/fission/interchange/tiling/peeling, and polyhedral loop transformation — presented above in full depth.

response.content:
# SSA Construction, Alias Analysis, and Escape Analysis: Technical Brief

## 1. SSA Construction

Static Single Assignment form requires that each scalar variable is assigned exactly once statically, with control-flow merges resolved by special pseudo-operations (φ-functions) that select among incoming definitions according to the predecessor block control flow took. Constructing SSA from a conventional CFG-with-mutable-variables IR involves two conceptually separate problems: **where to place φ-functions** and **how to rename variable occurrences** so each use refers to a unique definition. The literature offers several algorithmic families trading precision, time complexity, and implementation complexity.

### 1.1 Cytron et al. Dominance-Frontier Algorithm

The canonical construction (Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, Zadeck, 1991) is the standard against which others are measured.

**Dominance and dominance frontiers.** Node `d` dominates node `n` if every path from the entry to `n` passes through `d`. The dominator tree encodes this as a tree where each node's parent is its immediate dominator (idom), the closest strict dominator. The **dominance frontier** `DF(n)` is the set of nodes `m` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `m` but `n` does not strictly dominate `m` itself. Intuitively, `DF(n)` is the set of join points immediately beyond the region `n` dominates — the first points where control paths originating from (or passing through) `n` can reconverge with paths that did not.

**Why φ-placement needs DF.** A φ-function for variable `v` is needed at block `m` if two distinct definitions of `v` can reach `m` along different control-flow paths — i.e., `m` is a join point for defs of `v`. Cytron et al. show that the minimal set of join points for a single definition at `n` is exactly `DF(n)`. Because inserting a φ-function is itself a new "definition" of `v`, φ-placement must be computed as a fixed point: the **iterated dominance frontier** `DF⁺(S)` of a set of definition blocks `S`, defined as the limit of the sequence `DF(S), DF(S ∪ DF(S)), …`. Concretely, the algorithm maintains per-variable worklists of blocks containing a definition of `v`; it processes each block `n` on the worklist, inserts a φ for `v` at every block `m ∈ DF(n)` not already having one, and adds `m` to the worklist (since the inserted φ is itself a def). This is run once per variable (or once globally with per-variable bitsets), giving the standard algorithm `O(N²)` worst case in the number of blocks in pathological CFGs, though `DF` sizes are small in practice and the algorithm is near-linear on typical programs.

**Renaming.** After placement, renaming proceeds by a depth-first traversal of the **dominator tree**, which is the essential data structure ensuring correctness. For each original variable `v`, a stack of currently-visible SSA names is maintained. On entering a block: for each φ for `v`, push a fresh name onto `v`'s stack and record it as the φ's result; for each ordinary assignment to `v` encountered in order, push a fresh name. Uses of `v` are renamed to the top-of-stack name. On reaching each CFG successor `s` that has a φ-node for `v`, the current top-of-stack value is written into the appropriate φ-operand slot corresponding to the predecessor edge. On leaving a block (post-order), all names pushed within it are popped. This DFS-with-stacks exploits the dominance property directly: because every use is dominated by its (textually) nearest reaching definition's declaration point in the tree, a stack discipline correctly resolves "the most recent definition on the path from entry" without needing full dataflow iteration — renaming is linear in the number of variable occurrences (with amortized stack operations), after the DF⁺ computation.

### 1.2 Sreedhar–Gao Pruned / Sparse Dominance-Frontier Variants

The classical algorithm inserts φ-functions wherever `DF⁺` indicates a join of *definitions*, without checking whether the variable is actually *live* at that join — producing **minimal but not pruned** SSA: minimal in the sense that no fewer φs could capture all definition merges, but not pruned because some inserted φs are for dead values.

**Pruned SSA** eliminates φ-functions at points where the variable has no subsequent use (i.e., is not live-out of the merge into any path), typically by first running a live-variable dataflow analysis and intersecting the `DF⁺`-driven insertion with liveness: insert a φ for `v` at `m` only if `v` is live-in at `m` *and* `m ∈ DF⁺` of `v`'s def set. This avoids φ nodes for values nobody subsequently reads, shrinking the SSA graph and the renaming workload, at the price of needing liveness information up front (itself an `O(N)`-ish iterative dataflow pass, or computable via the same dominator-tree machinery).

**Sreedhar and Gao (1995)** go further with an algorithm avoiding explicit dominance-frontier set construction altogether, motivated by the fact that `DF` sets can be large (quadratic in the worst case) even though the eventually-needed φ placements are sparse. They introduce **DJ-graphs**: the dominator tree (`D`-edges) augmented with the original CFG's join edges (`J`-edges, i.e., edges `x → y` where `x` does not strictly dominate `y`). They define levels on the dominator tree and process J-edges bottom-up by level, propagating φ-insertion requirements upward only as far as necessary, which computes the **iterated join** set without materializing full dominance-frontier sets. This is often called the DF⁺-on-demand or sparse approach. Combined with a liveness check, this yields **semi-pruned** or **pruned SSA** directly, with better asymptotic behavior on CFGs where dominance frontiers are large but the live, "real" φ requirement is small (common in heavily-connected control flow such as switch-dispatch or exception handling regions).

**Minimal vs. pruned vs. semi-pruned terminology**, precisely:
- **Minimal SSA**: exactly the φs required by `DF⁺` over definition sites — correct and non-redundant with respect to merging *reaching definitions*, but may include φs for variables dead at the merge.
- **Pruned SSA**: minimal SSA intersected with liveness — no dead φs, smallest φ set consistent with correctness.
- **Semi-pruned SSA**: a cheaper approximation used by many production compilers (e.g., early GCC tree-SSA): a fast, non-iterative "quick" liveness-like pass identifies variables that are *never* live across a block boundary at all (purely local variables) and excludes them from SSA renaming entirely before running the Cytron DF⁺ insertion on the remaining globals; this avoids the cost of full iterative liveness while still prudently restricting the variable set that is SSA-named, trading some precision (it may still insert a few unnecessary φs for variables that are globally-but-not-locally live past a given join) for cheaper up-front analysis.

### 1.3 Braun et al. Simple/Linear-Time SSA Construction

Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leißa, Mallon, Zwinkau (2013) present a construction method designed for direct use during IR building (e.g., while parsing an AST), without ever materializing a dominator tree or dominance frontiers up front — valuable for JIT compilers and SSA-based IRs built incrementally (e.g., in simple one-pass front ends).

**Core idea: local value numbering with block arguments.** Each basic block maintains a map from source variable to current SSA value, populated as the block is built (standard **local value numbering**). A use of variable `v` in block `b` first checks `b`'s local map. If absent, the algorithm recursively asks: what is the reaching definition of `v` at the *start* of `b`? This becomes a per-block, per-variable memoized query `readVariable(v, b)`.

- If `b` has exactly one predecessor, the value is simply `readVariable(v, pred)` (recursing up the CFG), with no φ needed — this is the predecessor-based, demand-driven lazy resolution that avoids ever consulting dominance information explicitly; dominance is implicitly respected because the recursive predecessor walk only terminates at actual definitions.
- If `b` has multiple predecessors (a potential join point), a φ-function is tentatively created for `v` in `b` *before* its operands are known, and recorded in `b`'s local map immediately (to break recursive cycles during loop processing — this is the **incomplete phi** / "φ placeholder" technique). Only after insertion are the predecessor values resolved recursively and filled in as φ operands.
- Blocks not yet **sealed** (not all predecessors known yet, as happens when processing a loop header before its back-edge source is built) have their incomplete φs recorded for later completion once sealing occurs, at which point missing operands are filled in via further recursive `readVariable` calls.

**Phi simplification (trivial φ-elimination).** After a φ's operands are all known, the algorithm checks whether the φ is *trivial*: if all non-self operands are identical (ignoring the φ's self-reference, which can occur in loops), the φ is redundant and is replaced everywhere by that single common operand, and the φ is removed. This check must be applied transitively, since removing one trivial φ can make a user of it (another φ) trivial in turn — handled by maintaining use-lists and a worklist of φs to recheck. This mechanism is what gives the algorithm its "automatic pruning": no DF or liveness computation is needed, because unnecessary φs introduced speculatively at merge points are eliminated locally and cheaply as soon as their redundancy becomes apparent, converging to a form close to (though not always identical to) pruned minimal SSA.

**Complexity and trade-offs.** The approach is near-linear in program size for typical (non-pathological) CFGs since each variable read triggers a bounded recursive predecessor walk memoized per block, and runs without separate dominance/liveness prepasses — attractive for single-pass or incremental construction (used in libFirm, Cranelift's early SSA builder work, and various JIT front ends). Its disadvantage versus Cytron-style batch construction is that worst-case behavior on highly irregular CFGs (deep irreducible graphs) can be less predictable, and the sealing/incomplete-φ bookkeeping has to be implemented carefully to be correct across arbitrarily nested unsealed loop structures.

### 1.4 Memory SSA

Ordinary SSA covers scalar, register-candidate variables. **Memory SSA** extends the same φ-placement/versioning discipline to *memory state* as an opaque, monolithic (or partitioned) value, enabling optimizations like dead store elimination, redundant load elimination, and memory dependence queries to be phrased as SSA-def/use queries rather than full alias-oracle walks.

Memory is modeled with special pseudo-operations: `MemoryDef` (a store or call that may modify memory, versioning the memory state), `MemoryUse` (a load, which reads a specific memory version but does not create a new one), and `MemoryPhi` (merging memory versions at control-flow joins, placed by the same DF⁺ algorithm applied to the "memory variable" abstractly). Because treating all of memory as a single SSA variable is maximally conservative (every store versions the single memory value, serializing dependence information), practical Memory SSA (e.g., LLVM's `MemorySSA` pass) is built atop an alias analysis oracle: when inserting a `MemoryUse`, the def it's linked to is found by walking backward through `MemoryDef`s and using `MayAlias`/`NoAlias` queries (see Section 2) to skip defs provably non-aliasing with the load — a technique sometimes called **walking Memory SSA** or using it in conjunction with a **clobber-skipping heuristic**. This hybridizes the sparse SSA structure (cheap traversal, dominance-based reasoning) with a separate, possibly flow-insensitive alias oracle for precision.

### 1.5 SSA Destruction (Out-of-SSA Translation)

Because most target machine code and many back-end IRs do not support φ-functions natively, SSA must eventually be lowered back to a representation using ordinary mutable variables/registers via **copy insertion at predecessors** replacing φ semantics. Naively, each φ `x = φ(x₁ from B₁, x₂ from B₂, …)` is translated by inserting `x := xᵢ` at the end of each predecessor `Bᵢ`. This naive translation is unsound in the presence of two classical hazards:

**The lost-copy problem.** If a value feeding a φ-operand is itself defined in a predecessor block but that predecessor has multiple successors (critical edge), and the copy is inserted carelessly at the end of the block, a value live along the *other* successor edge can be incorrectly overwritten before it's used, because the copy was placed on a shared tail rather than isolated to the edge actually feeding the φ. The standard fix is **edge splitting**: insert an empty block on every critical edge (an edge from a block with multiple successors to a block with multiple predecessors) so that the copy for each φ-operand can be placed on a dedicated edge-specific block, decoupling it from unrelated control flow.

**The swap problem.** When multiple φ-functions in the same target block reference each other's predecessor values (e.g., `x = φ(y,…)`, `y = φ(x,…)` coming from the same predecessor), naive sequential copy insertion `x := y; y := x` destroys the needed value before it's consumed — the φ-functions execute logically **in parallel** (reading all old values simultaneously, then writing all new values), not sequentially. This requires **parallel copy sequentialization**: the set of copies implied by all φ's for a given predecessor edge must be treated as a parallel-copy instruction and lowered correctly, typically by constructing a dependency graph among the copy destinations/sources and either (a) using a temporary register to break cycles (standard technique: for each cycle in the copy graph, save one value to a temp, perform the chain, then restore from the temp), or (b) topologically ordering acyclic chains directly when no cycle exists.

**Coalescing.** Naive out-of-SSA translation produces one new temporary/copy per φ-operand, which is correct but inflates register pressure and inserts many redundant moves. **Coalescing** merges SSA names that are copy-related (connected by an inserted or φ-implied copy) into a single non-SSA variable when it is safe to do so — safety requires that the merged live ranges do not interfere (are never simultaneously live with conflicting values), checked via the SSA interference graph (two SSA values interfere if one is live at the definition point of the other and they are not equal). This is essentially a specialized form of **register coalescing** performed during SSA destruction (sometimes called *SSA-based coalescing*, as formalized by Sreedhar et al.'s "copy folding" and the Hack/Grund/Goos work on SSA destruction via *interference graphs of chordal form* — SSA's dominance structure guarantees the interference graph is **chordal**, which permits optimal / polynomial-time coalescing and register allocation in some SSA-based register allocators, as opposed to the NP-hard general graph coloring problem). Good SSA destruction algorithms (e.g., Boissinot et al.'s "Revisiting Out-of-SSA Translation") combine liveness-based interference checking, value-based (not just name-based) coalescing, and minimal parallel-copy insertion to produce near-optimal copy sequences in close to linear time.

---

## 2. Alias Analysis

Alias analysis determines, for pairs of memory references (pointers or more generally access paths), whether they can or must refer to overlapping storage. Its output gates the legality of nearly every memory-related optimization: load/store reordering, redundant load elimination, dead store elimination, register promotion of memory locations, and vectorization.

### 2.1 Andersen's Analysis (Inclusion-Based)

Andersen's analysis (1994) is **flow-insensitive, inclusion-based (subset-constraint)** points-to analysis. For every pointer-valued variable (and, in field-sensitive variants, every field/struct member), it maintains an explicit **points-to set**: `pts(p) ⊆ Locations`. Program statements generate **subset constraints** over these sets rather than directly computing values:

- `p = &a` ⟹ `a ∈ pts(p)` (base constraint)
- `p = q` ⟹ `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)` (copy constraint)
- `p = *q` ⟹ `∀ a ∈ pts(q): pts(a) ⊆ pts(p)` (conditional/load constraint)
- `*p = q` ⟹ `∀ a ∈ pts(p): pts(q) ⊆ pts(a)` (conditional/store constraint)

These constraints are solved by iterating to a fixed point, propagating elements through the subset-constraint graph (a directed graph where nodes are abstract variables/locations and edges denote "⊆"); since the constraint graph itself can grow dynamically as points-to sets grow (new edges activate when a dereferenced variable's points-to set gains a new member), the standard solution strategy uses a worklist algorithm with "online" edge addition. Andersen's analysis is proven to run in **O(n³)** worst case (cubic in program/variable size) because each of `O(n²)` possible points-to-set memberships may need to be propagated along `O(n)` edges; in practice, sparse/bitvector/BDD-based implementations (e.g., `bddbddb`) and incremental/demand-driven variants make it scale to large codebases, but it remains the most expensive of the classical whole-program aliasing algorithms. Its chief virtue is **precision**: because it tracks subset (not equality) relationships, distinct pointers can point to overlapping but non-identical sets, giving substantially better may-alias precision than unification-based approaches, particularly for programs with significant aliasing structure (containers, union-like patterns).

### 2.2 Steensgaard's Analysis (Unification-Based)

Steensgaard's analysis (1996) sacrifices precision for speed by using **equality constraints** instead of subset constraints: whenever two abstract locations are determined to be related by an assignment that in Andersen's formulation would create a subset edge, Steensgaard's algorithm instead **unifies** them into a single equivalence class, under the (more conservative) assumption that `p = q` implies `pts(p) = pts(q)` henceforth (not just `⊆`). The implementation uses a **union-find** data structure over abstract storage locations (often represented as simplified type structures with `ref`/`points-to` fields), achieving **O(n α(n))**, i.e., essentially linear (up to the inverse-Ackermann factor from union-find), and scales to very large codebases (originally demonstrated on whole-program C analysis at the scale of real OS kernels).

The precision loss is structural: once two variables are unified because one was ever assigned to or derived from the other, they are considered to point to exactly the same (merged, unified) abstract object for the *entire* remainder of the analysis — including program points where, flow-sensitively, their actual points-to sets might have since diverged. This is why Steensgaard's result is often characterized as giving a single global "points-to graph" per program (rather than Andersen's lattice of distinct points-to sets), and why it's suitable for "quick and conservative" alias oracles (e.g., as an initial fast pass or in time-constrained JIT contexts) but less suitable where optimization payoff depends on fine distinctions (e.g., disambiguating individual array/struct-field accesses).

### 2.3 Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA, as implemented in LLVM and used to justify C/C++'s **strict aliasing rule**, is a fundamentally different mechanism: rather than tracking points-to sets at all, it uses the **static type** of the access (the type through which a memory location is dereferenced) as a proxy for aliasing, under the rule-driven assumption that accesses through incompatible types cannot alias unless one of the types is `char`/a compatible "universal" type, or the types are related by C's compatible-type/common-initial-sequence rules for unions and structs.

LLVM encodes this via `!tbaa` metadata attached to load/store instructions, describing a type descriptor in a **TBAA tree** (a DAG expressing scalar type nodes and struct "path" nodes with explicit field offsets — "struct-path TBAA" refines plain TBAA to be field-sensitive by encoding access paths through aggregate types, not just the leaf scalar type). Two memory accesses are deemed `NoAlias` if their TBAA descriptors are proven incompatible according to the type-compatibility DAG (ancestor/descendant relation check), subject to the caveat that this reasoning is only sound under language rules the frontend guarantees (e.g., it is unsound for code that violates strict aliasing via type-punning through unrelated pointer casts, which is why `-fno-strict-aliasing` disables TBAA-based reasoning in Clang/GCC). TBAA is attractive because it's essentially free at the optimizer level (a metadata lookup and DAG traversal, no fixed-point computation) but its soundness is entirely contingent on frontend-enforced language semantics rather than a general, language-independent static analysis — making it a "trusted hint" mechanism layered on top of (and consulted ahead of, as a cheap filter before) more expensive pointer analyses.

### 2.4 Flow-Sensitivity, Context-Sensitivity, and Field-Sensitivity Axes

Three independent precision axes classify alias analyses, each with associated cost:

- **Flow-sensitive** analyses compute a distinct points-to/alias result at each program point (tracking how aliasing relationships change as the program executes, e.g., after a store that redirects a pointer); **flow-insensitive** analyses (both Andersen's and Steensgaard's as classically formulated) compute one aliasing summary valid at all program points, which is sound only if treated as an upper bound (may-alias) over the whole procedure/program, since it merges information across all control paths and all loop iterations. Flow sensitivity requires combining the constraint-based pointer analysis with a dataflow framework propagated along the CFG (often per-SSA-value when alias analysis is built atop SSA, using the fact that each distinct SSA name already demarcates a flow-sensitive "version").
- **Context-sensitive** analyses distinguish different call sites / call stacks when analyzing a function, avoiding the imprecision of conflating a function's behavior across all its callers (commonly implemented via cloning, call-strings, or the functional/summary-based approach of computing parameterized summary points-to effects per function, as in the classic Sharir-Pnueli / "functional approach" to interprocedural analysis); **context-insensitive** analyses (Andersen's and Steensgaard's base forms) merge all calling contexts of a function into one, which can produce spurious aliasing when, e.g., a function is called once with aliased arguments and once without.
- **Field-sensitive** analyses distinguish individual fields/members of a struct/object as separate abstract locations (so `p->f1` and `p->f2` are tracked as potentially non-aliasing even if `p` is the same), typically implemented by appending a field offset or field name to the abstract location identifier; **field-insensitive** analyses collapse an entire aggregate to one abstract location, so any store through any field conservatively aliases any load through any field of an object with the same base points-to information. Field sensitivity interacts with array handling too — most practical field-sensitive analyses are field-insensitive *within* arrays (collapsing all array elements to one location) because fully precise per-index tracking would require integrating with index/range analysis (effectively becoming a form of value-range or shape analysis).

Each axis can be mixed independently (e.g., LLVM's default scalar optimizations mostly rely on flow-insensitive, context-insensitive, but reasonably field-sensitive `BasicAA` plus TBAA; whole-program tools for bug-finding often use context-sensitive Andersen-style analyses at far higher cost).

### 2.5 Shape Analysis / Access-Path Based Alias Analysis

For heap-manipulating programs (linked lists, trees, recursive data structures), simple points-to sets are often too coarse because every node of a linked list can be field-insensitively or even field-sensitively conflated into one "the list" abstract location. **Shape analysis** (e.g., the TVLA framework based on 3-valued logic, or access-path-based approaches as in points-to analyses for Java using bounded-length access paths like `p.next.next`) tracks richer structural invariants: whether a pointer-based structure is acyclic, how many distinct objects it can reach, and disjointness properties between structures (e.g., that two trees rooted at different pointers share no nodes). This supports optimizations and verifications that plain points-to analysis cannot, such as proving a recursive traversal terminates, or that two recursive data structures are strictly non-aliasing (enabling, e.g., parallelization of independent tree traversals). The cost is substantially higher analysis complexity (often super-linear and sometimes exponential in naive formulations, mitigated by abstraction/widening in abstract-interpretation-based shape analyses), restricting practical use to targeted verification tools or specific compiler passes rather than general-purpose optimizer infrastructure.

### 2.6 Must-Alias vs. May-Alias

The fundamental output distinction underlying all the above: a **may-alias** result between two references means the analysis cannot rule out that they refer to the same location on some execution — this is the *conservative* default and is what blocks an optimization from proceeding (e.g., a store cannot be eliminated as dead if a later load *may-alias* it). A **must-alias** result means the analysis has proven the two references *always* refer to the same location on every execution reaching that program point — this is the stronger, enabling condition required for optimizations like store-to-load forwarding (replacing a load with the value of a prior store) or redundant store elimination across a may-aliasing but must-equal pair of accesses. Note the asymmetry: must-alias information is strictly harder to establish (often requiring flow-sensitive, sometimes path-sensitive reasoning, since "always the same location" is a universal claim over all paths) and is correspondingly rarer and used more narrowly than may-alias information, which suffices as the default "not disjoint" conservative fallback that keeps all other optimizations sound. A third category, **no-alias** (must-not-alias, i.e., provably disjoint on every execution), is what actually licenses aggressive reordering/parallelization and is the main payload of precision-oriented analyses like Andersen's or TBAA.

---

## 3. Escape Analysis

Escape analysis determines whether a dynamically allocated object's lifetime and visibility are provably confined to the allocating method/thread/stack frame, enabling allocation-elimination and synchronization-elimination optimizations that would otherwise be unsound in the presence of unrestricted aliasing.

### 3.1 Connection-Graph-Based Escape Analysis (Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira, IBM)

The classical algorithm underlying early HotSpot escape analysis (and originally developed for IBM's Java JIT research) is built on a **connection graph**, an abstract points-to-like graph constructed per method (and extended interprocedurally via summary application) with three categories of nodes:

- **Object nodes** representing abstract allocation sites (one node per `new` statement, standard allocation-site abstraction).
- **Reference nodes** representing local variables/fields that may point to objects.
- **Phantom/deferred nodes** representing objects possibly created by callees whose exact identity is unknown at the call site (used to make the analysis interprocedurally sound without full inlining).

Edges are of two kinds: **points-to edges** (reference node → object node) and **deferred/field edges** (reference node → reference node, or object → object via field edges, modeling aliasing not yet fully resolved, later "folded" to direct points-to edges as the graph is refined, i.e., the deferred edges serve a role like Steensgaard's unification deferral but within a richer graph structure that supports distinguishing escape states per node). The algorithm processes a method's statements in a single (or iterative, for loops) pass, building/updating the connection graph, and interprocedurally summarizes each method's effect on its connection graph (which nodes become globally escaping, which become argument-escaping) so that call sites can be analyzed via **summary application** without reanalyzing callee bodies each time (a form of the function/summary-based interprocedural analysis style, analogous to the context-sensitive handling discussed in alias analysis).

**Escape states** are computed per abstract object node by propagating escape information along the connection graph's edges to a fixed point:

- **NoEscape**: the object is reachable only from local references within the current method/compilation unit, never stored to a field of another escaping object, never returned, never passed to an unanalyzed callee. Fully safe for stack allocation and scalar replacement.
- **ArgEscape**: the object escapes the current method via being passed as a call argument (or returned) but is not proven to escape the *thread* or become globally visible — the callee might still only use it locally. This state allows some optimizations (e.g., thread-local reasoning, lock elision — see 3.6) but not full stack allocation if the callee's behavior is unknown or conservatively assumed to store it elsewhere.
- **GlobalEscape**: the object is stored into a static field, a heap field of an object already globally escaping, or otherwise becomes reachable from outside the current analysis scope entirely — no allocation-related optimization is sound.

The analysis proceeds as a **monotone dataflow fixed point** over the lattice `NoEscape ⊑ ArgEscape ⊑ GlobalEscape` (ordering by increasing visibility/conservativeness), propagated along connection-graph edges: an object's escape state is the join (least upper bound, most conservative) over all paths by which it becomes reachable from an escaping context.

### 3.2 Partial Escape Analysis (Graal)

Classical escape analysis as above is **all-or-nothing per allocation site**: if any control-flow path causes an object to escape, the entire allocation is conservatively treated as heap-allocated along *all* paths, even ones where it provably does not escape. Graal's **partial escape analysis** (Stadler, Würthinger, Mössenböck) removes this limitation by performing escape analysis **flow-sensitively along the control-flow graph using an abstract interpretation style over "virtual objects"**: an allocation is represented symbolically (not materialized) as long as the analysis can track it, and is only **materialized** (actually allocated on the heap, with a real object header and layout) lazily, exactly at the specific control-flow point/edge where it is forced to escape (e.g., passed to an unanalyzable call, stored into an escaping field, or merged with a materialized value at a control-flow join where the merge cannot be resolved virtually).

Mechanically, this is implemented as part of Graal's **partial escape analysis + virtual object pass**, which runs essentially as a sparse, SSA-aware abstract interpreter: each allocation produces a **VirtualObjectNode** carrying symbolic field values (themselves possibly other virtual objects, enabling recursive/transitive scalar replacement through object graphs); reads and writes to fields of a virtual object are resolved directly against this symbolic state (not through real loads/stores) as long as the object stays virtual; and a **materialization** node is inserted precisely at the control-flow edge forcing escape, after which the object behaves as an ordinary heap object from that point forward (with its then-current field values written out as an explicit allocation + stores sequence). The benefit is allowing scalar replacement and allocation elimination on the **common (non-escaping) paths** of a method even when a *rare* path (e.g., an exceptional branch, or a branch calling an opaque method) causes escape — the escaping branch pays the allocation cost; the dominant path doesn't. This directly interacts with speculative/profile-guided compilation in a JIT: Graal can additionally use branch-probability profiles to bias where materialization is "pre-emptively" inserted versus deferred.

### 3.3 Scalar Replacement of Aggregates

Once an object is proven `NoEscape` (or kept virtual under partial escape analysis for the relevant path), **scalar replacement of aggregates (SROA)** rewrites the object's fields as independent local scalar variables (SSA values), eliminating the aggregate's memory representation entirely. E.g., a non-escaping `Point{x,y}` object becomes two independent SSA-named scalars `x` and `y`, which then participate fully in standard scalar optimizations: constant propagation, value numbering, and crucially, further enabling SSA-based optimizations that cannot see through an opaque heap load/store pair. SROA is the mechanism that converts "this allocation doesn't escape" into actual code quality improvement; escape analysis alone (without SROA or stack-allocation) only provides lifetime information, not a rewrite. In LLVM, the analogous general-purpose pass is `SROA`/`mem2reg`-adjacent machinery operating on `alloca`s proven non-escaping/non-aliased, which is conceptually the same transformation applied to stack-frame aggregates rather than heap objects — the unifying requirement in both cases is a proof (from escape analysis or from alias analysis on the `alloca`) that no other reference can observe the aggregate's memory layout directly.

### 3.4 Stack Allocation Promotion

Independent of (but often paired with) scalar replacement, an object proven `NoEscape` can be **promoted from heap allocation to stack allocation**: instead of invoking the allocator (and later relying on garbage collection), the object's storage is carved directly out of the current stack frame (or a synthetic extension of it), with its lifetime automatically ending when the frame is popped. This is valuable when scalar replacement is not possible (e.g., the object's fields are accessed via dynamically-computed offsets, or the object is too large/complex to fully decompose, or it's passed by reference to an inlined/known callee that itself doesn't escape it but does need an addressable aggregate rather than independent scalars). Stack allocation removes both the allocation cost (bump-pointer or free-list allocator call) and, crucially, the garbage-collection tracing cost for that object (it's never enqueued as a GC root/heap object), directly reducing GC pause-time pressure in managed runtimes. This is the primary payoff historically cited for JVM/HotSpot-style escape analysis, though full stack allocation of arbitrary-sized/variable-lifetime objects requires the escape proof to also bound the object's lifetime to be no longer than the enclosing frame's — which is exactly what `NoEscape` certifies.

### 3.5 Interaction with Lock Elision / Biased Locking

When escape analysis proves an object is `NoEscape` with respect to **threads** specifically (sometimes tracked as a distinct dimension from "escapes the method," since an object might escape the method via being returned but still provably never be accessed by more than one thread) — more precisely, when the analysis proves the object cannot be observed or synchronized upon by any thread other than the allocating one — any `synchronized` block or monitor-enter/monitor-exit operation on that object becomes unobservable to other threads and can be **elided entirely** (lock elision / **monitor elimination**). This is sound because mutual exclusion is only semantically meaningful when contention is possible; if no other thread can ever obtain a reference to the object, the lock operations are pure overhead. HotSpot's escape-analysis-driven optimizations historically combined this with **biased locking** (a separate, profile/runtime-based optimistic locking fast path that assumes single-thread ownership and only falls back to full CAS-based locking on actual contention) — escape analysis provides the *static* guarantee enabling full elision in the provably single-threaded case, while biased locking provides a *runtime-adaptive* fallback for cases where staticescape analysis cannot fully prove thread-confinement but empirically most lock acquisitions remain uncontended. The two mechanisms are complementary layers of the same underlying goal (reducing synchronization overhead) operating at different certainty levels: static proof (escape analysis) versus optimistic runtime assumption with cheap correction (biased locking).
